templates.pattern: An atom has a mass number of [A] and an atomic number of [Z]. Calculate the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
templates.explanation:
Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number
= A − Z
= [A] − [Z]
= [RESULT]

Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. They have identical chemical properties but different masses.

templates.pattern: An atom has [P] protons and [N] neutrons in its nucleus. Calculate the mass number of the atom.
templates.explanation:
Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons
= [P] + [N]
= [RESULT]

The mass number is always a whole number. It represents the total number of nucleons in the nucleus.

templates.pattern: An element has two naturally occurring isotopes. Isotope 1 has mass [M1] and abundance [AB1]%. Isotope 2 has mass [M2] and abundance [AB2]%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of the element.
templates.explanation:
RAM = (M₁ × AB₁ + M₂ × AB₂) ÷ 100
= ([M1] × [AB1] + [M2] × [AB2]) ÷ 100
= [RESULT]

RAM is a weighted average of all naturally occurring isotopes. This is why RAM values on the periodic table are not whole numbers.

templates.pattern: An element has a relative atomic mass of [RAM]. A sample of the element has a mass of [MASS] g. Calculate the number of moles in the sample.
templates.explanation:
Moles = mass ÷ relative atomic mass
= [MASS] ÷ [RAM]
= [RESULT] mol

The mole is the fundamental unit of amount in chemistry. One mole of any element has a mass in grams equal to its relative atomic mass.

templates.pattern: An element has a relative atomic mass of [RAM]. Calculate the mass of [MOLES] moles of the element in grams.
templates.explanation:
Mass = moles × relative atomic mass
= [MOLES] × [RAM]
= [RESULT] g

One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles and has a mass in grams equal to the relative atomic or molecular mass.

templates.pattern: An atom of atomic number [Z] loses [CHARGE] electrons to form a positive ion. How many electrons does the ion contain?
templates.explanation:
Electrons in positive ion = atomic number − electrons lost
= [Z] − [CHARGE]
= [RESULT]

When an atom loses electrons it becomes a positive ion (cation). Metals typically form positive ions by losing their outermost electrons.

templates.pattern: An atom of atomic number [Z] gains [CHARGE] electrons to form a negative ion. How many electrons does the ion contain?
templates.explanation:
Electrons in negative ion = atomic number + electrons gained
= [Z] + [CHARGE]
= [RESULT]

When an atom gains electrons it becomes a negative ion (anion). Non-metals typically form negative ions by gaining electrons to fill their outer shell.

templates.pattern: The [N]th electron shell of an atom can hold a maximum of how many electrons?
templates.explanation:
Maximum electrons in shell n = 2n²
= 2 × [N]²
= 2 × [N*N]
= [RESULT]

Shell 1 holds max 2, shell 2 holds 8, shell 3 holds 18, shell 4 holds 32. This pattern 2n² determines electronic configurations.

templates.pattern: A sample contains [MOLES] moles of an element. Calculate the number of atoms in the sample. Give your answer as a multiple of 10²³. (Avogadro's number = 6.02 × 10²³)
templates.explanation:
Number of atoms = moles × Avogadro's number
= [MOLES] × 6.02 × 10²³
= [RESULT] × 10²³ atoms

Avogadro's number (6.02 × 10²³) is the number of particles in one mole of any substance. It is one of the most important constants in chemistry.

templates.pattern: A sample contains [ATOMS] × 10²³ atoms of an element. Calculate the number of moles of atoms in the sample. (Avogadro's number = 6.02 × 10²³)
templates.explanation:
Moles = number of atoms ÷ Avogadro's number
= [ATOMS] × 10²³ ÷ 6.02 × 10²³
= [ATOMS] ÷ 6.02
= [RESULT] mol

This is the reverse of multiplying by Avogadro's number. Both directions of this calculation appear regularly in GCSE and A-Level chemistry.
